title: Major progress on my voxel extraction shooter (v0.2): Full procedural city generation, smooth simplex terrain, dense 3-tier grass & ambient wildlife! [Video]
author: PumpkinUpstairs
selftext:
Hey everyone! 👋

Following the incredible feedback and reality checks from my previous post, I’ve spent the last few days implementing major architectural and visual upgrades for v0.2. 

Here is a full new gameplay video showing the updated world generation, the new procedural city system, dense undergrowth, and living atmosphere!

---

### 🏙️ What’s New in this Update (v0.2):

1. **Full Procedural City & Urban Ruins Generation:**
   * Expanded beyond isolated forest bunkers into **entire procedural city districts and urban ruin zones**.
   * Multi-building urban layouts, interconnected street grids, collapsed multi-story facades, and claustrophobic CQB alleyways generated dynamically at raid launch.

2. **Smooth Simplex Terrain Shader (No more pixelated grid artifacts):**
   * Completely replaced the old value noise with a continuous 2D Simplex Noise shader ($C^2$ smooth gradient).
   * Added smoothstep slope transitions between grass, moss-covered ledges, and cliff rock strata, eliminating harsh polygonal faceting and muddy patches.

3. **Multi-Tiered Volumetric Ground Cover**

4. **Ambient Reactive Voxel Wildlife (Fauna System)**

5. **Atmosphere & Urban Tactical Lighting**

---

### ❓ Would love your thoughts on the new gameplay clip:
* How does the transition between natural terrain and dense procedural city ruins feel to you?
* Does the combination of urban CQB, destructible voxel structures, and ambient wildlife hit the right balance of tension and atmosphere?

Really excited to hear your thoughts and critiques! Thanks again to everyone who shared advice on the previous post!

replies.author: bonsoir-world
replies.body: This is for sure more than just prompting AI. AI does procedural gen very well and very awfully at the same time. The terrain, density and visuals are all way to good here to be simple prompts.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
You're right about the dual nature of AI. If you just ask an LLM to "make a procedural world", you get unoptimized spaghetti code and flat, lifeless noise. 

The real work is in the architectural direction and constant iteration: breaking the project down into strict modular systems (Transvoxel SDF terrain, analytical Simplex shaders, greedy-meshing algorithms, GPU MultiMesh instance buffers), backing everything with a 340+ headless test suite so code doesn't drift, and spending hours tuning colors, lighting, foliage densities, and animal animation curves by eye.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
For the programming, I use Opus 5 and Sol 5.6 as an IDE pair-programmer alongside Godot 4.7 / GDScript. 

I use it primarily as an interactive assistant for drafting shader math (like the Simplex noise and slope blending), generating automated test suites, and speeding up complex procedural algorithms. The high-level architecture, game design, and visual art direction are all guided by hand, but having an AI agent in the IDE to write boilerplates and refactor GDScript makes solo development infinitely faster.

i like how you can destroy the environments but would like it to have more feedback/impact so it look less like blocks are disappearing and more like they are being destroyed.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
Regarding the destruction feedback: you’re right. Right now when a block breaks, it just disappears cleanly from the mesh. I’m currently working on adding proper "destruction juice" spawning 3D physics-based micro-debris chunks, concrete/plaster dust particles, and punchy impact audio so it feels heavy and tactile when you breach a wall. As for how the graphics were made: I actually didn't use Blender.

Vegetation, Fauna & Props: Created using MagicaVoxel (.vox files) and custom procedural mesh builders directly in Godot 4 that convert voxel data into optimized meshes and GPU MultiMesh arrays.

Terrain: Continuous Transvoxel SDF terrain textured with custom triplanar Simplex shaders written directly in Godot's shading language.

Atmosphere & God-rays: Powered natively by Godot 4's Vulkan renderer (SDFGI, volumetric fog, and anisotropic light scattering).

Using a pure voxel/code pipeline instead of traditional 3D polygon modeling in Blender keeps everything lightweight and allows the engine to modify and destroy geometry on the fly.

comments.author: Melbar666
comments.body: I am looking forward to play it some day, looks very promising. At first glance I am missing the effects and animations when firing.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
Thank you so much, hearing that you're excited to play it means the world to me! You're completely right about the shooting feel. In this early build, the weapon handling is just a basic placeholder raycast.  Juicing up the gunplay is my top priority for the next update: adding procedural weapon recoil kick, animated slide/bolt cycling, crisp muzzle flash lights, flying shell casings, and hit-spark particles. Making the weapons feel punchy, heavy, and satisfying is essential for a tactical shooter.

I'll make sure the next gameplay video has much heavier weapon feedback!

comments.author: MikeRadical
comments.body: looks crazy, is it a browser game? I loved ace of spades.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
To answer your question: it's a native desktop standalone PC game (built in Godot 4 / Vulkan for Steam/Windows/Linux), not a browser game. Running natively is what allows the engine to handle over 100,000+ dense foliage instances, volumetric god-rays, continuous Transvoxel terrain, and smooth 100+ FPS destruction without web browser performance bottlenecks.

Really glad the vibe reminds you of Ace of Spades, that classic tactical voxel energy is exactly what I'm aiming for!

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
The core plan is a tactical Extraction FPS (PvE / PvPvE) centered around high-stakes military raids into overgrown procedural exclusion zones, forgotten Cold War bunker complexes, and ruined cities.

I'm aiming for a gritty, tactical survival tone, military PMCs, trench networks, CQB bunker breaches, and environmental hazards, where the big differentiators are true voxel destructibility (blowing murder-holes in concrete walls, collapsing cover) and unpredictable procedural raids where nobody can memorize the map. Because the underlying engine is modular (climate biomes + procedural voxel architecture), the foundation has a lot of flexibility to explore different factions, ancient ruins, and underground complexes.

comments.author: Ysn123987
comments.body: Looks awesome. What are system reqs? What minimal graphics card for this voxel style?

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
Because the game is built in Godot 4 on the Vulkan (Forward+) renderer, here is what I’m currently targeting for system requirements:

Minimum Target (1080p - 60 FPS):

GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 (6GB) / GTX 1650 Super or AMD Radeon RX 580

Recommended (1080p/1440p 100+ FPS):

GPU: NVIDIA RTX 2060 / RTX 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600.

Why it runs efficiently:

The voxel buildings use greedy-meshing (combining coplanar block faces to drastically cut draw calls), the 100k+ grass clumps are handled on the GPU via MultiMesh instancing, and the terrain uses distance-based LOD streaming. So you definitely won't need a high-end beast of a PC to enjoy smooth voxel destruction!

replies.author: Crafty-Variety-7635
replies.body: I am curious about how much destruction. Whole buildings with per voxel collision or just ground collision.

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
It's full dynamic per-voxel collision on entire buildings, not just ground collision. Here is how the system works under the hood:

The buildings are made of 0.2m (20cm) micro-voxels. When an explosive or heavy bullet impacts a wall, the damaged voxels are destroyed, and a background greedy-mesher recalculates the local physical collision mesh in real-time. 

That means if you blow a hole through a concrete wall:

\-The hole is physically open: bullets, grenades, and players can shoot, see, and climb through it.

\-You can carve custom sniper murder-holes, blow open barricaded doors, or breach ceilings.

\-The structural integrity solver checks for load-bearing supports , if you destroy the foundation or columns holding up a room, the unsupported ceiling can physically collapse.

replies.author: Crafty-Variety-7635
replies.body:
Are you keeping track of buildings with ids so you only calculate physics on buildings near the player or weapon impact.  I have a similar system with a structural physics building solver also.

You can check it out here
https://www.reddit.com/r/godot/comments/1vzhuex/throwing_buildings_is_soooo_cool/

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body: Yes, exactly! Each building is an independent entity with its own bounding box. The structural physics and collision updates are strictly event-driven: they only trigger on the specific building that gets hit by an explosion or bullet, so there are zero physics calculations running on distant or untouched buildings. Awesome that you're building a similar structural solver! How are you handling the collapsed debris when a building section falls?

replies.author: Crafty-Variety-7635
replies.body: I have 2 physics systems, one for the voxel environment and then I convert the active falling voxels into box3d, with greedy-meshing, active physics on them. I also have a floating island checker to make sure falling blocks on top of falling blocks fall. I then convert inactive box3d elements back to voxels when at rest. There is lots of buffer copying between the systems

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs

replies.author: PumpkinUpstairs
replies.body:
What will set it apart as development progresses is the tactical extraction gameplay and destructive CQB:

Instead of a generic sandbox or arcade shooter, it's designed around high-stakes military raids with persistent stash progression, where procedural generation prevents players from memorizing static camping angles, and 0.2m voxel destruction allows you to physically blow murder-holes through bunker walls or collapse stairwells during intense gunfights. Polishing the weapon viewmodels, tactical animations, and sound design is the next big step to give the game its own distinct identity. Thanks for the honest push, it’s a great reminder to make the unique gameplay hooks stand out!
